[[File:Brownian surface.png|thumb|A single realisation of three-dimensional Brownian surface]]

A '''Brownian surface''' is a [[Fractal landscape|fractal surface]] generated via a [[fractal]] elevation [[Function (mathematics)|function]].<ref name=Russ >{{cite book|title=Fractal surfaces, Volume 1|first=John C.|last=Russ|year=1994|isbn=0-306-44702-9|page=167|publisher=Springer |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qDQjyuuDRxUC&dq=%22brownian+surface%22&pg=PA167}}</ref><ref name=xie>{{cite book|title=Fractals in rock mechanics|first=Heping|last=Xie|year=1993|isbn=90-5410-133-4|page=73|publisher=CRC Press |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lXElMU9_tIMC&dq=%22brownian+surface%22&pg=PA73}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Fractal growth phenomena|first=Tamás|last=Vicsek|year=1992|isbn=981-02-0668-2|page=40|publisher=World Scientific |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=InnD-GTUi0gC&dq=%22brownian+surface%22&pg=PA40}}</ref>

The Brownian surface is named after [[Brownian motion]].

==Example==
For instance, in the three-dimensional case, where two variables ''X'' and ''Y'' are given as coordinates, the elevation function between any two points (''x''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;''y''<sub>1</sub>) and (''x''<sub>2</sub>,&nbsp;''y''<sub>2</sub>) can be set to have a mean or [[expected value]] that increases as the [[Euclidean vector|vector distance]] between (''x''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;''y''<sub>1</sub>) and (''x''<sub>2</sub>,&nbsp;''y''<sub>2</sub>).<ref name=Russ /> There are, however, many ways of defining the elevation function. For instance, the [[fractional Brownian motion]] variable may be used, or various rotation functions may be used to achieve more natural looking surfaces.<ref name=xie /> 

==Generation of fractional Brownian surfaces==
Efficient generation of fractional Brownian surfaces poses significant challenges.<ref>{{cite book |authorlink1=Dirk Kroese |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=Berlin|pages=369–404 |arxiv=1308.0399 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-10064-7_12 |chapter=Spatial Process Simulation |title=Stochastic Geometry, Spatial Statistics and Random Fields |series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |date=2015 |last1=Kroese |first1=Dirk P. |last2=Botev |first2=Zdravko I. |editor1-last=Schmidt |editor1-first=V. |volume=2120 |isbn=978-3-319-10063-0 }}</ref> Since the Brownian surface represents a [[Gaussian process]] with a nonstationary covariance function,
one can use the [[Cholesky decomposition]] method. A more efficient method is Stein's method,<ref name="Stein">{{ Cite journal | author = Stein, M. L. | title = Fast and exact simulation of fractional Brownian motion | journal = Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics | year = 2002 | volume = 11 | issue = 3 | pages = 587–599 | doi = 10.1198/106186002466 | s2cid = 121718378 }}</ref>
which generates an auxiliary stationary Gaussian process using the [[circulant embedding]] approach and then adjusts this auxiliary process to obtain the desired nonstationary Gaussian process. The figure below shows three typical realizations of fractional Brownian surfaces for different values of the roughness or [[Hurst parameter]]. The Hurst parameter is always between zero and one, with values closer to one corresponding to smoother surfaces. 

[[File:Fractional Brownian surfaces for different Hurst parameter.jpg|thumbnail|center|upright=3.0|Fractional Brownian surfaces for different values of the Hurst parameter. The larger the parameter, the smoother the surface. These surfaces were generated using a [http://www.mathworks.com.au/matlabcentral/fileexchange/38945-fractional-brownian-field-or-surface-generator Matlab implementation] of Stein's method.]]
